newsitem.title: USA: American Air resumes flights after Clinton intervenes.
newsitem.headline: American Air resumes flights after Clinton intervenes.

text.p: American Airlines rushed on Saturday to put its planes back in the air and passengers into its seats after President Bill Clinton ended a 24-minute pilots' strike.

The airline immediately offered huge discounts in a bid to attract replacements for the tens of thousands of passengers who had rebooked with rival carriers to avoid getting caught by a strike, and delighted travelers boarded planes after being told they were no longer stranded.

Clinton stepped in shortly after union leaders ordered all of American's 9,300 pilots to walk off the job at midnight Friday (0500 GMT on Saturday). The short-lived strike followed five days of intense negotiations with management which failed to bring agreement on a new four-year labor contract.
Clinton established a Presidential Emergency Board, effectively postponing any possible strike at the nation's second-largest airline for another 60 days.
American officials said they were delighted Clinton had blocked the strike, which would have cost the economy as much as $200 million a day and the airline about $30 million a day.
The move upset many pilots but brought huge relief at airports across the country.

"I am very happy he intervened. No worries," Emily Ghio, a 16-year-old from California, said as she hugged her parents and then boarded an American flight from Los Angeles to Boston to compete in a fencing competition at the Junior Olympics.
Just minutes earlier, as pilots at the airport marched in single file to set up picket lines, Ghio and hundreds of other passengers thought they were stranded.
But Clinton's announcement was quickly relayed across the country and virtually all scheduled flights were resumed.
In a bid to regain passengers who had jumped ship as the strike loomed, American announced a series of sales and promotions.

They included discounts of up to 50 percent on 21-day excursion fares and 40 percent on portions of tour packages, a doubling of frequent flier mile credits and 45 percent discounts for cargo customers.

Although the strike only lasted a few minutes, American lost tens of millions of dollars in recent days as passengers rebooked their flights for this long Presidents Day holiday weekend and virtually ignored the carrier as they made travel plans for the next month and beyond.

Clinton's decision was certain to delight the Caribbean tourist industry, which is in its peak winter holiday season and would have been battered by a strike, and cities across the country where American is strong.

American accounts for 20 percent of the nation's air travelers, carrying 200,000 passengers per day on about 2,200 flights. If the strike had continued, the airline would have placed virtually all of its 90,000 employees on unpaid emergency leave.
Airline officials said they would have most of its domestic flights up and running on Saturday but that the full international service would take a day or two to resume.
American had canceled virtually all of its international flights on Friday because it did not want its planes to be stranded abroad in the event of a strike.
Some pilots said they had mixed feelings about the postponement of the strike.
"I don't like what the president has done, but in a way I am also relieved financially. It's good for my family," pilot Tom Crews said at Dallas-Fort Worth, American's home airport.
But Crews and other pilots warned that Clinton's appointment of a presidential board did not mean the threat of a strike was over.

Under the terms of the Railway Labor Act, the board will draw up a settlement proposal within 30 days. Both sides will then have 30 days to act on its recommendations or reach their own settlement. If they fail to do so, the union will be free to begin a strike while the airline can impose a lockout.
